content.p: In the spring of 1822 an Ottoman fleet and army landed on the Aegean island of Chios and set about punishing its Greek Christian population for a rising it had mostly avoided. By the end of the summer, according to one account, only 1,800 of 117,000 Christian inhabitants remained. The sources describe large numbers killed, tens of thousands of women and children sold into slavery, and survivors who fled westward, many never to return.

No source agrees with another on the figures. Estimates of the dead run from 25,000 to more than 50,000, and a scholarly summary says as many as 100,000 islanders were killed, enslaved or displaced. What the sources do share is the picture of a rich, privileged island that had mostly stayed out of the Greek war of independence and was then punished as though it had joined it.
content.h2: An island that had much to lose
content.p: Chios sat only a few miles from the Turkish mainland. HistoryNet describes a light-handed government and a garrison that kept quiet. The island's famous product was mastic, a translucent resin from small trees at its southern end. Chian merchants, according to the ICWA writer, who lives in an island village, sold silk, wine, citrus and other luxury goods and built business communities across the empire, Europe and the Black Sea. The same account says the island enjoyed relative political autonomy, religious freedom and relaxed taxation, and that its leaders hesitated to join the Greek revolt because they knew how much they could lose.

The Korais Society of New York adds that because of the mastic trade, which supplied the sultan, the islanders had more privileges than Greeks anywhere else. Its history also notes the School of Chios, founded in the eighteenth century, and the churches and mansions that wealth built.

When the revolution began in 1821, a Hydriot squadron arrived to urge Chios to join. Island leaders refused, according to ICWA, but the Turks afterwards held Metropolitan Platon, his archdeacon and about 40 elders as hostages in the prison of Chios castle. HistoryNet gives the same general picture: some islanders did join the rebels in 1822, but the vast majority declined, saying they could contribute little and lived within sight of Turkey.

In 1822 a second attempt was made. ICWA says a Chian seeking glory, Antonios Bournias, persuaded Lykourgos Logothetis, the chief of neighbouring Samos, to lead it. The Greek Herald puts the Samian landing at 10 March 1822, with 1,500 men, and says the locals rose and the Turks fell back to the citadel. The ICWA writer calls the venture ill-conceived: the insurgents roused people from the countryside and attacked the castle and Muslim establishments.

When word reached Constantinople, ICWA reports, the sultan told Admiral Kara Ali to devastate the island he called ungrateful. The order, as ICWA relays it, was that infants, women over 40 and men over 12 should die unless they became Muslims. The captives held in the castle prison were then hanged, from trees in the main square of Chios town, Vounaki Square. A marble obelisk at the square's edge, engraved with the city's sphinx, bears the names of the metropolitan, the archdeacon and 56 other leading islanders put to death within ninety minutes.

HistoryNet gives a different, shorter sequence. It has the Turks send 1,000 soldiers in response to the rebel arrival and the Greeks answer with 1,500 of their own. The sultan then dispatched 15,000 further men, largely volunteers hoping to loot, and the small Greek contingent fled and left the roughly 120,000 islanders defenceless. A Flinders University chapter describes the event as a betrayal of a neutral population, and notes that people were killed, enslaved or displaced first by Greek revolutionaries and then by the retaliating Ottoman fleet.

The Ottoman fleet arrived on 30 March 1822, according to The Greek Herald and the Korais Society, which gives the force as seven thousand soldiers under Kara Ali Pasha. ICWA says that day was the Thursday of Holy Week, days before Easter. The ICWA writer, drawing on island memorials and conversations with museum staff, says the ships fired on the town and reduced it to rubble. People fled to the countryside and hid in caves, basements and tombs, while the weak and the elderly were killed in their homes. Troops brought severed heads and ears to the Ottoman governor, hoping for rewards.

Three thousand women and children took refuge in the monastery of Agios Minas, not far from the estates of Kampos, and others went to Nea Moni, the eleventh-century monastery that is now a UNESCO World Heritage site. On Easter Sunday, ICWA says, Turkish forces surrounded Agios Minas and fired cannon at its walls. After six hours they broke in and killed everyone in their path, set fire to the church and threw burning mattresses into the cistern where the last survivors hid. Nea Moni was pillaged and, according to the same account, hundreds of monks were killed. The tower-village of Anavatos, built on a cliff, was besieged by 1,500 Turks on 10 April 1822; a municipal brochure quoted by ICWA says its women chose death to avoid dishonour.

The ICWA writer also quotes Richard Calvocoressi, a descendant of a prominent Kampos family, who wrote in The New Statesman that the killing was "essentially a holy war". He recounts that his ancestor Ioannis Kalvokoresis was mutilated, finger by finger, because he would not surrender his gold or abandon his faith. That is a family account, not a court finding.
content.h2: Counting the dead and the enslaved
content.p: The sources set the loss against different baselines and reach different totals.

ICWA and The Greek Herald give 42,000 killed. The Greek Herald, counting 117,000 Christian inhabitants, adds that about 50,000 were taken captive and 23,000 escaped to rebel-held Greece or to Western Europe, and that the Turks lost around 600 men. ICWA says the troops sold about 52,000 women and children into slavery. Greek City Times in one article gives about 25,000 murdered and more than 45,000 taken to the slave markets of the Ottoman Empire; the Korais Society also gives 25,000 slaughtered and "almost twice that number" enslaved. HistoryNet says estimates of the slaughtered ran upward of 50,000, with an equal number enslaved. Smarthistory, a museum-education site, says only that according to reports as many as 30,000 people were killed, with others starved and many enslaved.

The Times of London, in an editorial of 1822 reproduced by the Chios Societies, spoke of a population of 120,000 reduced to about 900, with many of the remainder dying daily of pestilence from unburied corpses. The Chios Societies, an advocacy group, used it to answer those who called the horror exaggerated. The Flinders chapter's phrase "as many as 100,000" covers killed, enslaved and displaced together.

The ICWA writer cites the filmmaker Eirini Steirou's observation that official history, by focusing on those killed, often understates the fate of the roughly 52,000 women and children who filled the slave markets of Constantinople and Smyrna. The same piece says influential Chians living abroad used their contacts to organise fundraisers to buy back captive women and children. The Flinders abstract adds that the massacre also drove a forced migration of Chians into Ottoman centres, many of them held as slaves or kept in the name of re-education, a part of the story it calls under-examined.

Three months after the landing, on the moonless night of 6 June 1822, the Greeks answered. Konstantinos Kanaris, from the island of Psara, approached Kara Ali's flagship, according to ICWA, while the admiral celebrated the end of Ramadan aboard his 84-cannon ship. Kanaris and his crew fastened a fire ship to its stern, and the fire reached the powder store. Greek City Times says Kanaris had thirty-six men with him and that the admiral jumped into the water but was killed by a falling spar. ICWA says the explosion killed the admiral and 2,000 Turks, plus about 700 prisoners in the hold; the Korais Society says 2,300 Ottoman sailors and officers died.

The attack brought no relief to Chios. ICWA says it brought a new wave of destruction, including the mastic villages such as Olympoi, which until then had been spared. By the end of summer, that account says, the island was reduced to rubble and ash. Kara Ali was buried in the Ottoman graveyard in Chios castle. In summer 1824 the island of Psara was invaded and destroyed by Ottoman forces seeking to cripple the Greek fleet and avenge Kanaris's attack.

ICWA says the European press covered the massacre at length, given how well known the island was and how far its merchants' network reached. HistoryNet argues the massacre was a turning point: until then the European powers had declared neutrality and many had profitable trade with the Ottomans, but the bloodbath disgusted their people and leaders, and Britain threatened to withdraw its ministers from Constantinople. Greek City Times says European reporting concentrated on atrocities against the Christian population and drew on a humanitarian narrative already shaped by campaigns against the slave trade.

The ICWA writer quotes the scholar Yianni Cartledge, who calls the massacre a pivotal event that "humanized" Greeks in Western eyes, and argues that Europeans identified with the victims partly because elites regarded ancient Greeks as their cultural forebears. The same account notes that the killing of so many Christians provoked rhetoric reminiscent of the Crusades. It also cautions that the British historian Roderick Beaton describes the war overall as a "descent into savagery" in which both sides routinely used extreme violence. HistoryNet itself describes the Greek capture of Tripolis the year before, where one observer estimated Greeks killed 8,000 Turks on the first day and 2,000 civilian refugees were murdered in a ravine.

Eugene Delacroix, aged 26, finished Scenes from the Massacres of Chios, which Martin Kramer says was first shown at the Salon on 25 August 1824. Kramer writes that Delacroix relied on press reports and conversations with a French eyewitness, and that the painting's subtitle as submitted was "Greek families await death or slavery, etc." The canvas is nearly fourteen feet high and almost twelve feet wide, and has belonged to the Louvre for 150 years. Smarthistory's presenters note that large canvases were normally reserved for history and myth, and that this one shows a contemporary event with no hero. Greek City Times says Delacroix meant to arouse sympathy and political support for the Greek cause. The ICWA writer observes that the painting is steeped in Romanticism and Orientalism and that Delacroix never visited Chios. The Korais Society adds that Victor Hugo wrote the poem "Enfant de Chios" after the massacre.

On the island the event remains central. The Chios historian Athina Zacharou-Loutrari told the ICWA writer that there are no Chians who have not heard of it. The Massacre of Chios Museum at Agios Minas opened in November 2021, part of the Greek Church's bicentennial programme; according to the architect Manolis Vournous, quoted by ICWA, the bishop wanted to stress the sacrifice of so many people and its effect in turning international opinion toward the Greek cause. Its main artefact is a door from the monastery's outer wall, scarred by bombardment. A three-day torch relay across the island marked the 200th anniversary.

The Church of Greece has also canonised Metropolitan Plato of Chios and 43 others, priests, deacons, hieromonks and monks, who were martyred by Ottoman troops on Holy Friday 1822, according to OrthoChristian. The ICWA piece records that the memory now feeds present-day unease over Turkey, whose coast lies 3.5 nautical miles from the island at its nearest point. Refugees from the destruction helped found Ermoupoli on the island of Syros, which became a shipping and trade centre.
